findings.title: The amendment leaves two conflicting user-facing onboarding entry points
findings.description: The amendment says “`/cf:onboard` stays the entry point for now, with no brownfield path,” while the Overview, Design Goals, and Adoption flow all name `sq onboard` as the brownfield entry point. The project’s own process journal (`project-documents/user/notes/000-process-journal.md`, 20261022 entry) records the opposite ruling: “`cf onboard` and `sq onboard` side by side is not acceptable: two command surfaces are already confusing for new users. The work may be split internally between the tools, but the user sees one entry point, either `cf onboard` or `sq onboard`.” This architecture therefore violates a standing process decision without recording a superseding ruling. The document must either name one user-facing entry point or explicitly record why the journal’s ruling no longer applies.

findings.title: The read-only detection report is specified without a concrete public interface
findings.description: The detection report is the central cross-repo contract: `sq onboard`, `cf init`, and `cf next` consume it, and slice 271 exposes it as CLI + MCP. Yet the architecture does not define the JSON shape, the outcome enum, the fact names, or whether the opt-out is reflected in the report. Slice 271 defers “command names” and “how the profile is delivered” to slice design, but this is a cross-repo contract with an external consumer, not an internal naming choice. The same omission applies to the prompt-delivery primitive: “fetch the adoption prompt from cf … with the comprehension doc’s path filled in” has no defined request/response contract. Define both primitives’ wire formats (including versioning) in the architecture before squadron builds against them.

findings.title: The architecture describes a three-way detection outcome but the implementation has a four-value state machine
findings.description: The amended design says detection derives “greenfield, brownfield or already planned” with only an opt-out stored. The shipped implementation still models `"" | in_progress | complete | declined` (`packages/core/src/config/ConfigKeys.ts:28`) and the resolver’s decision order is persisted state → already planned → source volume (`packages/core/src/adoption/adoptionResolver.ts:50-64`, `packages/core/src/adoption/adoptionOutcome.ts:30-49`). The architecture relies on slices 269–271 to collapse this, but the “Current State”, “Anticipated Slices” (original plan), and Technical Considerations sections still describe the old four-value model, the persisted “adoption state”, and build-time detection. A reader cannot tell which of the two designs is authoritative. Remove or clearly quarantine the superseded state-machine description.

findings.title: The retroactive-marker rules and the existing-state slice plan are excluded from the rework that consumes them
findings.description: The rework list (268–272) removes the persisted adoption state and the `cf build` path, but slice 271’s success criteria require “the prompt fills the comprehension path” and slice 273 depends on 271–272 to produce an existing-state slice plan. The slice plan’s “Deliberately not in this rework” section excludes “retroactive slice entries (cf check, the review gate and the plan parser)” — yet those shipped components (`packages/core/src/introspection/retroactiveRules.ts`, `packages/core/src/introspection/parsers/slicePlanParser.ts:23`) remain the only mechanism implementing the architecture’s retroactive contract. The exclusion is acceptable only if the shipped parser stays stable; the architecture does not say so, and the removal of `adoption.state` touches the same navigation/parser path. State explicitly that 269–270 must not alter the marker parser, gate skip, or checker rules, or fold their preservation into the rework.

findings.title: The guide prompt’s mandatory “Adoption Facts” contract is not covered by the rework
findings.description: The guide prompt shipped in ai-project-guide still says: “If the section is missing, stop and say: ‘The Adoption Facts section is missing; cf build should always supply it…’ Do not continue on any path” (`project-documents/ai-project-guide/project-guides/prompt.ai-project.system.md:452`), and it still branches on raw probe JSON and a CF-only path (`:453-464`). The architecture’s Technical Considerations says these branchings “go away” and slice 272 aligns the guide, but the architecture does not specify the new prompt’s input contract (what replaces Adoption Facts, and whether the prompt still hard-requires it). The rework ships cf primitives before the guide release carrying the reworked prompt exists; until that guide lands, the delivered prompt contract is broken. Define the new prompt-delivery payload and the minimum guide version explicitly, not just “slice 272 aligns it”.

findings.title: The document’s guide-version facts contradict the implemented minimum
findings.description: The Dependencies section says cf releases “require at least v0.22.2”, but the implemented constant is `MIN_GUIDE_VERSION = '0.22.6'` (`packages/core/src/guides/guideMinimum.ts:5`). The architecture is the contract used by slice design and release gating; shipping it with a stale minimum risks a release that believes it is compatible with a guide that is not. Bring the version floor in the architecture to the value actually enforced, or state that the floor is raised by slice 272 and is not yet fixed.

findings.title: “Already planned” detection is narrower than the architecture claims
findings.description: The amended rule says “Already planned” covers “an initiative plan, an architecture doc or a slice plan.” The implementation matches the initiative plan only by the exact filename `001-initiative-plan.*.md` (`packages/core/src/introspection/ArtifactIntrospector.ts:34`) and architectures only by `NNN-arch.*.md` / `NNN-hld.*.md` under `project-documents/user/architecture` or `project-documents/user/project-guides` (`packages/core/src/detection/planningArtifacts.ts:15-17,57-65`). A project using a different initiative-plan index, an architecture in another directory, or an HLD with another prefix is detected as brownfield and will have adoption write artifacts over existing work. The document treats “the files say whether a project is planned” as a reliable invariant; the current matcher does not make it reliable. Either broaden the detection rule to the set of artifact kinds CF actually understands, or state the exact filename conventions as part of the contract.

findings.title: The scope includes conventions reconciliation and docs/ADR mapping although the initiative’s core goal does not depend on either
findings.description: The Scope paragraph includes “and, last, conventions reconciliation and docs/ADR mapping,” while the stated core goal is only that “`cf next` points at the first piece of new work” after adoption. Conventions reconciliation is explicitly the highest-risk item in the slice plan (266: Risk High, Effort 4/5), depends on the unresolved #123 audience split, and introduces a new persisted resolution format plus agent-driven semantic comparison. Docs mapping (267) is a separate discoverability feature. Both are already shipped as slices 260–267 and are declared outside the rework, so keeping them in the initiative’s Scope enlarges the architecture without contributing to the stated outcome. Cut both from this architecture’s Scope and track them under their own architecture, or state explicitly why they are load-bearing for adoption.

findings.title: Detection’s history and CI facts are produced but never used to decide an outcome
findings.description: The report includes “history” and “CI”, but the outcome is decided from the planning-artifact check plus source volume; the shipped implementation likewise computes history via a 5-second git timeout (`packages/core/src/detection/history.ts`) and CI recognition without letting either affect the outcome. This is consistent with the “facts in core, judgement in the prompt” principle, but it means the report carries relatively expensive facts that mostly duplicate what the prompt can observe. If they are genuinely intended for the agent, say so; otherwise they are removable cost on a primitive that `sq onboard` will call on every run.
